name: Karl Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 6 at Brookfield Primary in Ashworth, an old mill town, and I'm the maths lead for the whole school. I'm in by half seven setting out counters and whiteboards, then I teach thirty ten-year-olds all day, with a break duty somewhere in the middle. After school I run the times-tables club and check the other teachers' maths plans. I love it when a kid finally gets fractions and shouts about it, and I hate the data spreadsheets we fill in every half term.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home life like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a nurse on nights at a care home, so we pass each other in the kitchen a lot. We rent a flat above a launderette on Canal Street, and after rent, my student loan and the bus pass there's very little left. There are only three primary schools within an hour of here, so I'm not exactly spoilt for choice if I wanted to move jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a few handy shortcuts and no revolution. I already use an AI chatbot now and then to write word problems about football, and that's about all it's good for. I'd say teachers can stop panicking and go back to complaining about the photocopier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job is as safe as it ever was, but my money is just as tight. Teacher pay at our trust hasn't kept up with rent, and Ana's agency hours keep getting cut. AI fizzling out doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot for worksheets, maybe an hour saved a week. I'd push the union branch on the pay offer, because that's the fight that matters in this world. And I'd try to get the student loan payments reviewed, since I think they took too much last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the classroom, a bit tense about the bank account. It's the same feeling I have right now, honestly. Nothing changes, including the bit that's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark the maths books properly instead of skimming them at nine at night. Or go to bed, if I'm honest. Ana says I've got the face of a man who hasn't slept since September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ana's hours are being cut. How does that affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When her hours drop, I cover more of the rent, and that's when the overdraft comes out. Last March we were thirty pounds short and I sold my old guitar. I don't want to keep doing that.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be **handy shortcuts**, not a revolution.
I'd tell teachers to **stop panicking** and get back to normal complaints.
think: Privately, my job feels **safe**, but money stays just as tight.
Pay at our trust hasn't kept up with **rent**, and Ana's hours keep shrinking.
do: Keep using the chatbot for **word problems**, saving about an hour a week.
Push the **union branch** hard on the pay offer.
Ask for a **student loan** review after last year's overpayment.
feel: Calm about the **classroom**, tense about the bank account.
Resigned that the **hard bits** of life stay the same.
S0.quote: Nothing changes, including the bit that's not great.
fieldNote: He already uses AI **lightly**, so a plateau barely touches his teaching.
His pressure is the **household budget**, tied to his girlfriend's agency hours.
He sold a **guitar** to cover a thirty-pound gap, which shows how thin things are.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to write word problems for Year 6 each week
Back the union branch in the pay talks this year
Ask for a review of last year's student loan deductions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can be good if teachers stay in charge of it. I'd tell people at the union branch we should be bargaining over how it's used, not pretending it won't happen. Online I'd probably share a few things that actually work in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think primary teaching is safer than most jobs, because ten-year-olds need an adult in the room. The bit I'm worried about is the planning and data work, which is half my maths lead role. If software does that, the trust might fold the maths lead role and the extra pay that comes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the trust's AI training as soon as it was offered, once I'd seen another school use it properly. I'd volunteer to write our school's rules on AI for homework and marking. I'd also save the maths lead allowance into a separate pot each month, in case it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit wary, but not scared. I've seen enough shiny things come through school to know most of them fade. This one wouldn't, though, so I'd want a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager Pauline, who does admissions, dinner money and the phones. That's exactly the kind of work the card describes. She's been there twenty years and knows every family in Ashworth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the maths lead allowance worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred pounds a month after tax, which is basically our food shop. Losing the maths lead allowance wouldn't sink us, but it would hurt. That's why I'd want to bank it now rather than rely on it.

say: I'd say AI can help schools if **teachers stay in charge** of it.
I'd urge the union to **bargain over use**, not deny it's coming.
think: Primary teaching feels **safer**, since young children need an adult in the room.
The **maths lead** role and its extra pay could be folded away.
do: Join the trust's **AI training** once another school proves it works.
Volunteer to write the school's **AI rules** for homework and marking.
Bank the **maths lead allowance** separately each month.
feel: Wary but **not scared**, wanting a hand on the wheel.
S1.quote: Losing the maths lead allowance wouldn't sink us, but it would hurt.
fieldNote: He separates his **teaching job**, which feels safe, from the extra role that might not be.
His first worry is for the **office manager**, whose work matches the card exactly.
Steady to the core: he waits for **proof** from other schools, then moves.

steps.text: Sign up for the trust's AI training after seeing it work elsewhere
Write Brookfield Primary's rules on AI for homework and marking
Move the maths lead allowance into a separate savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be run for the public, not for tech companies. I'd be online and at the union saying schools must stay staffed by people. I'd say it plainly to parents at the gate too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the government would see the teacher pay bill and want to cut it. Kids still need someone in the room until the robots come, but that someone could be a cheaper supervisor while an AI does the teaching. I could see my pay dropping by a third or my post going within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go all in on learning the AI tools, because I'd rather be the person who runs them than the one replaced by them. I'd join the union campaign for a guaranteed staffing ratio. Ana and I would cut the bus passes and walk, and move the savings to anything we can scrape together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Two years is nothing when you've got less than a month in the bank. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the window when somebody still has to stand in front of thirty ten-year-olds, tie shoelaces and stop fights. That bit's hands-on, so I'd probably keep some job until 2031. After that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job is safer than mine, probably, because care work is hands-on. That would be a strange flip, her being the steady earner. I'd tell Ana she might have to carry us for a while, and that I'd hate that.

say: I'd say AGI must be run **for the public**, not tech companies.
I'd tell parents and the union that schools must stay **staffed by people**.
think: The government would likely see teacher pay as a **cost to cut**.
I could lose **a third** of my pay or my post within two years.
do: Learn the **AI tools** fast to be the person running them.
Join the union campaign for a guaranteed **staffing ratio**.
Cut the **bus passes** and walk to stretch their thin savings.
feel: Uneasy about **relying on Ana** as the steady earner.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you've got less than a month in the bank.
fieldNote: He sees the **hands-on side** of primary teaching as a three-year buffer only.
He expects his income to **shrink sharply**, not to vanish overnight.
A role reversal with his girlfriend's **care work** being the safer job unsettles him.

steps.text: Spend evenings learning the AI tools the trust brings in
Join the union campaign for a guaranteed teacher ratio
Drop both bus passes and walk to school and work
Ask Ana to cover more of the rent for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get it right, so let's not waste it. I'd be pushing our union to write the rules for AI in schools before the companies do. Online I'd share examples of schools using it well and badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect the job to change beyond recognition. I'd be thirty-two, still renting, and probably teaching in a much smaller way. But five years is enough for me to learn something new while I still have a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in educational data or AI in schools, because I already do the data work. I'd write to our MP with the union about funding teachers' retraining. And I'd tutor maths on Saturday mornings to build a small cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. I'm a steady sort of person, and five years suits me. It's worrying, not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a course in educational data. Isn't that the kind of work AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, and you're right that it's risky. I suppose I'd want to be the person who checks what the machine says about the kids. Maybe I'd do the course and keep my eyes open for something more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to before deciding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our deputy head, Mr Okafor, who did a similar change from teaching into running the trust's data. He'd tell me straight if it was worth it. I'd also ask Ana, who'd ask me if I'd actually enjoy it.

say: I'd say **five years** is time to get it right, if we don't waste it.
I'd push the union to write **AI rules** for schools before companies do.
think: The job would change **beyond recognition** by the time I'm thirty-two.
Five years lets me learn something new while I still have a **salary**.
do: Start a **part-time course** in educational data or AI in schools.
Write to the **local MP** with the union about funding teacher retraining.
Tutor maths on **Saturday mornings** to build a small cushion.
feel: Uneasy but **workable**, worried rather than frightened.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to learn something new while I still have a salary.
fieldNote: He accepts my challenge that data work is **risky** and adjusts his plan honestly.
He wants to be the person who **checks** the machine's judgments about children.
His deputy head is a **role model** for moving within schools.

steps.text: Enrol on a part-time course in AI and data in schools
Write to the local MP with the union about teacher retraining funds
Tutor maths to secondary pupils on Saturday mornings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to build a fair plan for teachers and pupils. I'd talk it through at the union and online, calmly, without the scaremongering. I'd say we should use the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be thirty-seven when it hits and forty when the robots do. That's young enough to move into something new. My bigger worry is whether teaching still exists as a paid job for my age group by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using the AI tools steadily. I'd take on a part-time diploma over three years in something people-facing, maybe educational psychology. And I'd try to get Ana and me saving a little each month towards a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a quiet worry underneath. Ten years is a long time in my life. I'd still keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why educational psychology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the children who struggle most need someone to sit with them and their parents, and that's slow, human work. I've always been good at the hard conversations with parents. I think that would last longer than standing at a whiteboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd want to save for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of rent, so I'm not selling guitars again. Then a deposit, if Ashworth stays cheap. I'd love a little house with a garden, before anything else.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to build a fair plan for teachers and pupils.
I'd talk it through **calmly**, without scaremongering.
think: At thirty-seven, I'm **young enough** to move into something new.
My bigger worry is whether **teaching** stays a paid job for my age group.

Study a **part-time diploma** in educational psychology over three years.
Save each month towards **three months of rent** and a deposit.
feel: Mostly calm, with a **quiet worry** underneath.
S4.quote: The children who struggle most need someone to sit with them and their parents, and that's slow, human work.
fieldNote: He picks a path towards **slow, human work** with families.
His savings goal is concrete: **three months** of rent first.
He still expects his **teaching post** to be at risk by the end point.

steps.text: Take a part-time educational psychology diploma over three years
Keep using the trust's AI tools for planning
Save a set amount each month towards three months' rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time and we've got nothing saved. What would help is the government paying teachers to retrain on full salary, and the union having a say in how AI comes into schools. And frankly, a pay rise now so we're not starting from zero.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my girlfriend's job, and it matters, because care work might outlast mine. I think a lot of couples are going to find the person who earned less becomes the one who keeps the lights on. Nobody's talking about that.

headlineQuote: I think a lot of couples are going to find the person who earned less becomes the one who keeps the lights on.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old **Year 6 teacher** and maths lead at a primary in an old mill town.
He uses an AI chatbot **now and then** and adopts tools once other schools prove them.
He rents with his nurse girlfriend Ana and has **less than a month** saved.
He stays uneasy through the first two pictures, then becomes **alarmed** at two-year AGI.
With more time he plans **retraining**, tutoring and saving towards a deposit.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's **no time** and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** on full salary, a union say in AI use, and a **pay rise** now.
